allowlist.reason: Hardware check: reads /proc/meminfo for system stats

Daemon-reachability boundary: this module forwards MCP tool calls to the daemon, which is the graph authority. Every filesystem touch here is about reaching that authority, never about answering in its place — no tool result derives from any of them. Three classes, each pinned to its whole expression: (1) the loopback bearer token at <kin_dir>/daemon.token, read so the forwarded request can authenticate; (2) repo binding, walking up from the working directory for the .kin layout marker to locate that token, which precedes any graph consult because it decides which daemon to talk to; (3) revival, resolving and spawning the known kin-daemon executable via KIN_DAEMON_BIN, the current exe's directory, the cargo target dir, and PATH, a `which` equivalent open-coded to avoid the dependency. The head-generation marker is the daemon's own published counter and only keys a within-session memo; a missing marker reads as generation 0, which costs cross-generation invalidation and never substitutes for a graph answer. Pinned rather than whole-file so any newly added filesystem primitive or subprocess in this module fails the guard The revival wait is split into its own helper so the spawned child handle outlives every exit it can take and reaches the detached-daemon reaper exactly once; its `&mut std::process::Child` parameter is process-lifecycle plumbing with no answer surface.

Config/capability IO: probes the local model cache directory for reranker availability now and for whether this install ever fetched the model; never reads repo content and is not a semantic answer path

Config/capability IO over the local embedding-model cache, the same root retrieval_profile.rs probes for the reranker. This module mirrors the loader's own cache layout to say whether the runtime embedding-model download has happened, is in flight, or will never happen: it tests whether a KIN_EMBED_MODEL_ID names a local directory, because such an id short-circuits the hub fetch and reporting it as a pending download would announce egress that never happens, and it walks the model's cache directory to sum the bytes already there, skipping symlinked snapshot entries so a resolved snapshot is never counted twice and bounded by a fixed entry budget. Those bytes are the numerator of a progress line on init, resources inspect, graph status and doctor; nothing here reads repository content and no result of it feeds locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. Pinned by exact expression so any newly added filesystem primitive in this module fails the guard until it is re-justified.

Telemetry consent boundary: the only filesystem touch in the locate authority path is the presence of the consent marker, which gates telemetry and never contributes to the ranked answer. Pinned so any other filesystem primitive in this module fails the guard

Known violation under repair, not a boundary claim. Unlike every other entry here, these reads ARE the answer authority: `kin spec list` and `kin spec show` resolve their result by walking and parsing .kin/specs/*.json, which is exactly what the Zero File-Search Authority Rule forbids on a query path. The entry exists so the violation is visible, owned, and dated rather than invisible, which it was until this module entered the scanned query set: nothing had ever reported it. It is not evidence the path is graph-backed and must not be read as one. The reason it cannot simply be fixed is storage, not wiring: the pinned registry crates carry no home for a spec. kin_model::Spec is a bare data struct, GraphStore composes EntityStore, ChangeStore, WorkStore, ReviewStore, VerificationStore, ProvenanceStore and SessionStore and none of them has a spec method, and kin-db imports SpecId without using it. Mapping a spec onto a WorkItem would drop constraints, affected systems, validation requirements and the free-string scope, so the faithful fix is a SpecStore in kin-model and kin-db, which is a bottom-up registry publish. Tracked on the internal board for the command and for the store substrate; both pins and this entry come out when the query path reads graph truth. Pinned to the seven exact expressions rather than the whole file, so the debt cannot grow: any newly added filesystem primitive in this module fails the guard. Re-dated from 2026-10-31 to 2027-01-29 on 2026-09-03. The original date was set while neither zero-file-search guard graded a pull request, so it was a tracking date rather than a merge blocker. kin#1448 moved both guards into fast-gate-lint, which carries the required "Fast gate lint and policy" context and no job-level if, so from that landing the expiry blocks every kin pull request on the day it fires, whatever that pull request touches. The fix is the SpecStore train described above: kin-model, then kin-db, then a registry publish, carrying a GraphSnapshot format version, which is not schedulable against the old date. Measured on 2026-09-03 against the current pins: still no SpecStore in kin-model 0.7.23 or kin-db 0.7.96, and kin-db still imports SpecId at types.rs:15 without using it. The new date is kin-cli's own review day under the staggering this guard now recommends, so it is not a day any other owner's entries share.

Repository selection boundary: resolves symlinks on a repository root so a client-supplied workspace root and the process working directory compare equal when they name the same repo (/tmp against /private/tmp on macOS, tempdirs under /var/folders in fixtures). It decides which repository to bind, before a binding exists and before any graph is consulted, so it precedes the answer path rather than serving it: no file contents are read and no query result derives from it. The error case falls back to the path as given rather than treating failure as absence, so it is not an existence probe. Pinned to the whole expression, so a bare canonicalize that did read failure as a signal, or any other filesystem primitive in this module, still fails the guard

Install-diagnostic boundary: kin health reports on the local installation, so the environment is its subject rather than a source of semantic answers. The line this pin enforces is that environment probes are a diagnostic boundary while repo-content reads are not, and every pinned expression was checked against it individually. Four classes: (1) install artifacts — the kin-daemon binary beside the current exe or in the cargo target dir, the VFS shim's metadata and its four-byte object header, the shell hook, the editor extensions directory; (2) environment config — the shell rc, of which two shells have more than one, since zsh's interactive .zshrc carries the hook while the always-read .zshenv carries the PATH line, and bash's .bashrc carries both while the login file a bash login shell reads (.bash_profile, .bash_login or .profile, first one only) carries the PATH line again, and doctor reads every one of them so an install that put the PATH line where a non-interactive or login shell can see it is not reported as missing it, and the AI-client MCP configs for Claude, Cursor, Codex and Antigravity, which are read to check the kin server entry and never for their surrounding content; (3) repo binding — the layout-discovered repository root is compared against the repository argument recorded in client config, and that root is first resolved to its canonical form, because the config writers record the canonicalized path and an unresolved root makes the check reject setup's own write wherever the two forms differ, which is every Windows install (the \?\ verbatim prefix) and any symlinked ancestor. The resolution takes a path already produced by layout discovery, reads no repository content, and its result is only ever compared, never returned as an answer. The setup-ledger fingerprint check belongs to this same class: it re-reads the client config bytes setup itself wrote to prove the on-disk entry is still the recorded one, and probes the recorded repository's existence before trusting the record, both feeding a comparison and never an answer; (4) a projection audit — read_dir over .kin/runs listing session workspaces left materialized. That last one is a filesystem read by necessity rather than by shortcut: it detects materialized state that reconcile has not reclaimed, and a graph that believed those sessions closed would report nothing, which is the exact failure the check exists to catch, so the traversal audits the projection against graph truth instead of standing in for it. Semantic readiness itself comes from daemon-owned embedding state, not sidecar presence. A fifth class, host assessment: two absolute-path subprocess probes (pgrep for the syspolicyd pid, ps for its CPU share) sample the macOS binary-assessment daemon so a saturated assessor is named as the cause of machine-wide launch stalls instead of surfacing as random tool hangs; they read scheduler state about the host, never repository content, and no output feeds a semantic answer. A sixth class, severity discrimination: four probes that decide whether a check reports a failure or reports nothing wrong, each testing for the presence of an artifact rather than reading one. The kin-vfs driver beside the managed binaries separates a shim the installer deliberately removed on a host that cannot run projection from a shim missing where projection is installed. The repository's daemon endpoint record separates a repository no daemon has ever started for from one whose daemon left its record behind unreachable. A .kin entry the layout already refused separates a partial or corrupt repository from a directory that simply is not one, and it is a probe for the marker directory, never a read of anything inside it; the layout, not this probe, decides what a repository is, and it has already answered before the probe runs. The fourth resolves two paths to their canonical form so the managed toolchain directory can be recognized as itself rather than as a repository someone failed to initialize, which is the same comparison-only use as class (3) and returns no answer. None of the four reads repository source content, and each exists so a correct install stops being reported as broken. No pinned expression reads repository source content. Pinned rather than whole-file so this module is falsifiable at every site and any newly added filesystem primitive fails the guard A seventh class, driver loadability: the kin-vfs driver is resolved beside the running binary, in the managed bin directory and on PATH, and the one candidate that is a regular file is executed with --help, stdin closed, and judged on whether the process reached its own code rather than on a zero exit, because the shipped driver takes a subcommand and exits 2 on a healthy install while a loader refusal exits 127 or dies at spawn. Existence is not loadability: an archive has shipped a driver needing a newer glibc than the host carries, and only running it produces the loader's message, which doctor then reports verbatim. The probe runs a binary that is part of Kin's own install, reads nothing from any repository, and its result decides between absent, loadable and unloadable rows. The managed bin directory's presence is tested for the same diagnostic reason: doctor --fix writes a PATH line for that directory only when it exists, so the check reports which of the two cases the install is in instead of promising a PATH entry for a directory nothing populated. An eighth class, projection reach: one read of the home directory and an lstat of each of its first few entries, taken only when the shim is injected into this process, stopping at the first entry that answers. Both calls are deliberate syscalls through whatever the loader has inserted, and their subject is the projection layer rather than any repository. Every other probe this row takes is inside the repository, which is the one path an engaged shim is certain to serve, so a shim answering an error for paths under the home directory read as healthy in the same shell where git exited 128 reading $HOME/.config/git/config. The stat matters beside the read, because the observed failure was for paths under the home directory and a probe that only listed it would miss the case it exists for. It is an lstat rather than a stat, and it walks several entries rather than one, so that a dangling symlink or a file removed between the listing and the probe cannot report a healthy machine as a broken projection. Neither call reads repository content, neither result is returned as an answer, and the pair exists so the projection row stops reporting health it never measured. A ninth class, hook liveness: the projection row reads the shell hook Kin itself installed and the shell rc that sources it, to answer whether a NON-KIN process in this shell would receive the VFS shim (FIR-2501). It has to read them rather than infer from the environment, because the hook's own `kin()` wrapper strips the two preload variables from every kin invocation, so the one process asking the question is the one process guaranteed not to carry the answer; measuring the preload here is what made a correct install report itself broken. The hook file is compared byte for byte against the bytes this build would install, so a stale hook is not read as a current one, and the rc is scanned only for the source line and never for its surrounding content. Both are install artifacts Kin wrote, both feed a comparison rather than an answer, and neither touches repository source. This is the same environment-config boundary class (2) already draws for `check_shell_path`, which reads the same rc files one row over.
Git export boundary: probes the output path's git layout to decide open-vs-init before materializing graph truth as git objects. Explicit output boundary, not a semantic answer
Git ingestion boundary: open_repo probes the .git layout before mining commit history into graph relations. Co-change relations are read back from the graph, never from this traversal
IO Boundary: notification delivery and its own suppression state; answers no semantic query and never reads repository content

Notification identity boundary; answers no semantic query and never reads repository content. The std::process:: matches outside run_action are an ExitCode import, a PID used for notification request uniqueness, and process exit. run_action is function-pinned because it is the notification action boundary: a button press runs the managed kin with a fixed argument vector chosen inside this file and never supplied by the caller, after confirming that managed binary exists. It derives nothing from what it runs and cannot serve locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename.
False positive: no filesystem access; the std::process:: match is an ExitCode import for the platform dispatch stub

Daemon process-boundary module end to end: bounded compatibility probes and their process-tree containment, capture, cancellation, and cleanup. It reaches and validates the daemon that owns graph authority and never derives a semantic query answer from filesystem or subprocess output. The file is dedicated to this boundary, so a whole-file exemption is reviewable; any future answer logic belongs elsewhere and requires removing or narrowing this exemption.

Daemon process lifecycle boundary with zero answer-authority surface. The exact expression pins cover process construction, readiness records, port records, PID records, and Linux process-table inspection; each reaches or supervises the daemon that owns graph truth and never derives a semantic answer. The PID record is read to establish that a daemon is still running, which is a liveness question about a process rather than a question about repository content: it can only withhold a restart, never produce or repair an answer. ManagedInstallSpawnFence::acquire is separately function-pinned because it is an install-mutation boundary: it binds the configured executable and update lock, rejects replaced or retired install roots, and serializes daemon spawn against uninstall. It reads only install/process identity metadata and cannot answer locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. The rest of this single-module crate remains scanned, and exact pin counts make any added occurrence fail closed. The death note and the daemon-log append are the same boundary read in the other direction: a daemon ended from outside cannot log its own cause, because the reaper's SIGTERM grace is shorter than the daemon's shutdown and the SIGKILL that follows lands while the arm that would print a shutdown line is still unpolled. These write that cause into the repository the daemon served and read it back, so a failed request can name a killed daemon instead of quoting a socket error. They carry process lifecycle facts only and answer no question about repository content. The open-transaction marker is the third instance of the same lifecycle boundary: the daemon publishes the phase and last beat of a write transaction it has open into .kin/daemon.transaction, the reaper reads it to tell a busy daemon from a wedged one, and the CLI reads it, together with the durable authority receipt, to classify a commit whose reply was lost as landed, still running, or gone. The four expressions pinned for it write, read and retire that one marker; the temporary-file removal is shared with the death note, which is why its count is two. They carry process lifecycle facts only, and none of them reads repository content or feeds a semantic answer. The boot-cost record is the fourth instance of the same lifecycle boundary and the narrowest: a daemon that has just finished opening a store writes what that open cost into .kin/daemon-boot-cost.json, and the next CLI spawn reads it back to size the idle window it gives the daemon it is about to start. It exists because the process that can measure an open is not the process that needs the number, and a fixed window shorter than a store's own cold start expires the daemon between two commands so the next one pays the whole open again. The three expressions pinned for it write, retire and read that one marker under its own local name, so its counts are separate from the death note's and the transaction marker's rather than folded into them. It carries a duration and nothing else, and can only lengthen or shorten how long a daemon idles; it never reads repository content and cannot produce, rank, fill or repair an answer to locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. The approaching-commit announcement is the same boundary again, written by the client rather than by the daemon. A commit and the ambient reconcile tick both admit the whole working copy, so whichever publishes first makes the other's publication redundant, and the tick already stands down for a commit it knows about. It cannot know about the one commit that matters most here, the one that had to start the daemon, because that commit reaches its handler only after the store has opened and the first reconcile round has already decided. The client therefore writes the announcement before it does any of its own work and withdraws it on the way out, and the daemon reads it back on the round that is about to decide. It carries a pid and a timestamp and nothing else. It can only withhold one ambient publication that a commit is about to make redundant, never produce, rank, fill or repair an answer to locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename, and it is bounded twice over: the record expires on its own, and a round stands down for a bounded number of consecutive rounds whatever the record says. Its four expressions are pinned under their own local name so its counts stay separate from the death note's, the transaction marker's and the boot cost's rather than folded into them. The kill record is the fifth instance of the same lifecycle boundary, and the cgroup readings are what let it say anything true. A daemon the kernel kills writes no note at all, so the reaper that already waits on every daemon this process started records the kill against the store that daemon served, and every surface that later meets a dead daemon reads it back instead of quoting a socket error. The two cgroup files it reads are the host's own memory accounting under /sys, not repository content: they say what this container's cap is and how many processes the kernel has killed inside it, sampled once before a daemon is started and again when it is found dead, because a counter read only after a death cannot say the kill it counts was this daemon's. Neither reading, and neither the write nor the read of the record itself, touches a file in the repository or feeds locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. They can only add a sentence to an error the caller was already receiving. The install-mutation fence that used to be exempt as a whole function is now pinned by expression instead, one pin per primitive, so its body is scanned again. The trade is worth making for the reason the guard's own falsification harness gives for the two bodies it reground before this one: a whole-body exemption swallows anything planted inside it, and a probe that lands there reports a blind spot the file does not otherwise have. The primitives are unchanged in what they do. They resolve the configured install root and the daemon binary to their canonical forms, refuse a symlinked or replaced root or binary, and take the update lock as a regular file, re-checking both after the lock is held so a swap during admission is caught. Every one of them reads install and process identity metadata, none reads repository content, and none can produce, rank, fill or repair an answer to locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. The sweep-interruption tally is the sixth instance of the same lifecycle boundary and the smallest: one number, written by the daemon after a sweep ends and read back by the next daemon to decide whether to queue another. It moved here from the daemon because three surfaces outside the daemon now have to say the same thing about it, and a second spelling of the same file in each of them is exactly the duplication the cgroup readers were moved down here to end. The two expressions pinned for it read and write that one file under its own local name. It carries a count and nothing else, it can only withhold an enrichment sweep or add a sentence to a report the caller was already receiving, and neither it nor anything derived from it touches repository content or feeds locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. The cgroup half of that boundary now goes through one injectable reader rather than three scattered opens: the limit, the usage, the peak and the kill counter are all resolved by walking from this process's own cgroup up to the hierarchy root, and the resolution itself is pure over that reader so every container layout is tested without one. That is why a single pinned expression replaces the three this entry used to name. The per-process footprint reader is the seventh instance of the same boundary and reads the host's own memory accounting under /proc rather than repository content: for one pid it takes the proportional set from smaps_rollup, the private set from smaps, or the resident-minus-shared pair from statm, whichever the kernel publishes. It exists because the daemon's budget used to SUM resident sets across its process tree, which charges every shared page once per process that maps it and reported 25.3 GiB inside a container hard-capped at 12 GiB, refusing background embedding on a box that had room (FIR-2653). The three names are joined into one path per pid, which is why a single pinned expression covers them; every one is a question about how much memory a process holds, none names an entity or reads a file in any repository, and nothing derived from them can produce, rank, fill or repair an answer to locate, search, context, trace, review, xref, or rename. The serving record is the same lifecycle boundary once more: a daemon publishes that it is alive, with the kernel's OOM counter as it stood, and retires it with its endpoint. A copy left behind by a process that is gone is the evidence that the daemon never reached the line which would have removed it, and the next start settles what that means. It names no entity and carries no repository content, and without it a daemon that outlived its spawner died unobserved and every surface reported the silence as a normal exit. A third record, .kin/lsp-refused-enrichment, is the same boundary once more and sits beside the sweep tally for the same reason: it holds what this store's last enrichment sweep offered the graph and did not get published, plus what it published whose endpoints' embeddings were left uninvalidated, written by the daemon that ran the sweep and read back by the MCP envelope in another process later. It carries three counts and a timestamp, names no entity and no relation id, and cannot answer a locate, search, context, trace, review or xref; it can only qualify one. Last writer wins, an unparsable record reads as absent so it can never itself become the degradation it reports, and a sweep that publishes everything retires it. Pinned by exact expression rather than whole-file so any added occurrence fails closed.

Daemon RPC surface. This file is the answer authority every agent, editor, and CLI reaches, so it is scanned in full and only the explicit IO-boundary bodies are excused. npm_registry_routes and router_with_rotation_tokens materialize package-registry directories; the rotation-aware router is where that body now lives, because extracting it moved the directory setup out of router_with_auth_and_shutdown, and an exemption that stayed with the old name would have excused nothing. router_with_auth_and_shutdown_internal is the delegating wrapper this branch added above it for the publication-control administrator token. health reports local runtime diagnostics; ensure_loopback_token manages the loopback credential. None derives a semantic query answer. The two expression pins cover a graph-owned blob lease metadata accessor and the durable authority publication-record probe. Locate, search, context, trace, impact, review, verify, MCP handlers, and every newly added handler remain scanned by default.

Supervisor process lifecycle boundary. The supervisor owns the daemon process, not any query answer, and each excused body is one of four classes. Endpoint records: the pid and port files, written through a temp-and-rename and removed only by the process that owns them, plus the url and canonical-path helpers that read them back. Singleton locks: the lifecycle guard file and its owner stamp, which decide whether another supervisor is already live. Install and process identity: the loopback auth token, both provisioning it and reading it back to present as this process's bearer credential when it calls a supervisor, same-binary comparison against the running executable, the log length and mtime probes, re-exec of the supervisor binary, and the reaper that kills rogue daemons. Registration payload and health: the repository record sent to the control plane and the local status report. None of these reads repository content, and no query result derives from any of them. Function-scoped rather than whole-file so the rest of the module, and anything added to it, stays scanned; the single expression pin is a struct field holding the lock file handle.

Shared per-repository runtime capability boundary. try_acquire_repository_runtime_authority canonicalizes the exact .kin root before it opens the never-unlinked daemon.lock and daemon.lifecycle inodes, so a capability acquired for one repository cannot be replayed while opening another. It writes only the caller-owned opaque process stamp after the exclusive lock is held and answers no repository query. Function-scoped so the owner-stamp validation, retry policy, public wrappers, Drop behavior, and any newly added filesystem access remain scanned by default.

Daemon lifecycle boundary: starting, finding, and stopping the process that holds graph authority. Five classes, all excused per function. Singleton coordination: the lock owner reader and short-lived lifecycle guards that serialize endpoint operations beside the shared runtime capability. Endpoint publication and ownership: the pid, port, and owner components are written atomically, read back, and removed only after owner-bound proof; the named ownership helpers make that proof independently testable without adding query authority. Binary resolution and liveness: locating and validating the exact kin-daemon executable and probing whether an endpoint is answering before spawning another. Bounded macOS process ownership: the private launchctl capture, stable process-group guardian, deadline, and cleanup helpers. Platform registration and migration: the digest-addressed LaunchAgent plist, exact legacy-authority inspection, staged replacement, rollback, and non-macOS no-op counterparts, which is why two public names carry a count of two. Every path here reaches, supervises, or registers the authority and answers no repository query. The expression pins are the process handle declaration and the capture file's Drop cleanup; neither produces an answer. Function-scoped so the remainder of the module stays scanned.
allow_match: use std::process::{Child, Command, ExitStatus, Output, Stdio};
use std::os::unix::fs::{MetadataExt as _, OpenOptionsExt as _, PermissionsExt as _};

allowlist.reason: Daemon state persistence boundary. The excused bodies write and read back state the daemon owns about itself, never repository content. Snapshot and marker persistence: the generation marker, the vfs version record, the mcp transaction log, and the coordination event log, each written through a temp-and-rename with an explicit directory fsync so a crash cannot leave a torn record, which is what the two cfg-gated sync_directory_metadata bodies and the two `open` bodies are. Failure accounting: the persisted failure count and its marker file. Graph-to-disk projection: staging and finalizing the canonical read index from graph truth, invalidating it, and asking whether the durable index and marker already describe the generation being loaded so startup can skip republishing bytes it would have rewritten unchanged. That reuse probe is a question about a derived artifact this same module publishes, never about repository content: it decides whether to rewrite the projection, and a false answer costs a redundant rebuild rather than a wrong answer. Authority pinning: resolving the registered local repository authority roots. The two expression pins are lease metadata accessors, which return graph-owned workspace state and only share a name with the filesystem probe. One resolves the registered sibling workspaces at startup; the other names the workspace whose semantic overlay language-server enrichment is published into, so those relations survive the process that found them. Pinned on the exact expression with a count rather than by function, so a third one, filesystem or not, fails the guard until it is justified here. Derived-sidecar disclosure: load_validated_vector_index asks kin-db to install the persisted vector index and probes for that same sidecar's presence beforehand. The probe decides nothing about the answer to any query and cannot change what the graph returns; the sidecar either installed or it did not, and kin-db reports both a missing sidecar and a rejected one as the same negative. It separates those two so a rejected index is announced as the discarded work it is instead of reading as a repository that never had one, which is the whole of FIR-1959. Nothing is read from the file, no content is recovered from it, and a probe that lied in either direction would change only the wording of a health report. Derived-coverage disclosure: record_embedding_coverage_complete, record_embedding_pass_drained, and write_embedding_coverage_marker publish a marker recording that this store's embedding fill once reached whole coverage, and embedding_coverage_ever_complete reads it back. The two recorders differ only in their evidence: one re-reads the live counters, the other is called by a pass that drained its own queue and therefore cannot lose to work admitted in the moment after, which is FIR-2203. The marker is written by the daemon that finished the fill and read only by the readiness report, which needs it to tell a store filling for the first time apart from one that held full coverage and lost it. It records a fact about work this same module did, names no entity, carries no repository content, and cannot change what any query returns; a probe that lied in either direction would change only whether a health check reads pending or stale, which is FIR-2103. Hosted vector projection: remove_derived_vector_file and replace_derived_vector_file retire and republish the local projection of a hosted vector artifact, and read_bounded_vector_artifact_file reads that projection's bytes back to hand to kin-db's decoder. The StorageBackend object is the authority here, and these three only materialize and retire its local copy; a sidecar kept from another backend generation on an ephemeral pod disk would let the next open serve an object the backend never handed over, which is why the projection is cleared rather than trusted. The republish is a temp-and-rename with an fsync of the staged file and then of the containing directory, the same shape write_generation_marker above uses, and the failed-write arm removes only the staged temp it created. The read is bounded by an explicit byte ceiling and names both the label and the path on every failure, so a missing artifact reports which artifact and where instead of a bare io error. None of the three names an entity, recovers repository content, or can change a locate, search, context, trace, review or xref answer: kin-db decodes and verifies the bytes they move, so a lie in either direction costs a refused attach rather than a wrong answer. Function-scoped rather than whole-file: this module is large and holds far more than its persistence paths, and all of that stays scanned.

Repository authority lease accessor, not a filesystem probe. The one scanned `.metadata()` is `RepositoryAuthorityState::metadata()`, which returns the graph-owned repository-v6 authority envelope; this module reads the workspace set out of it to find one workspace's base target and semantic overlay. It shares a method name with the filesystem metadata probe in the shared deny set, which is the only reason it appears here. Nothing in this module answers from the filesystem: it reports whether an open serves a workspace base from the persisted materialized graph section or folds it out of history, and every fact it reports comes from the authority envelope and the change map header the open already holds. Pinned by exact occurrence count rather than by exempting the surrounding function body, so any new `.metadata()` call, filesystem or not, fails the guard until it is re-justified. The module's only filesystem primitives are in `#[cfg(test)]` code the scan does not read: a Git fixture that seeds a repository for the section-detection test, and the ignored FIR-3064 open-cost harness, which discovers a store named by an environment variable and shells out to `ps` for a resident-set reading.

Durable bookkeeping marker published beside the authority head, not an answer authority. The excused bodies read and write .kin/kindb/last-admission, which records when a complete exact-tree admission last succeeded and how many artifacts it covered. It is written only where an admission actually completed and read only by freshness surfaces, which is what lets `kin graph status` state how far graph truth has fallen behind instead of printing an all-clear over a store admitted months ago. The record names no entity, carries no repository content, and cannot change what any query returns: a reader that lied in either direction would change only the wording of a freshness line, never a locate, search, context, trace, review, or xref answer. Publication is a temp-and-rename with an fsync of the staged file and then of the containing directory, the same shape write_generation_marker and read_generation_marker in crates/kin-daemon/src/state.rs use for the authority head marker this sits beside, and the two cfg-gated sync_directory_metadata bodies are that directory fsync. Routing through a shared boundary helper instead was not available: kin-core exposes no public atomic-write path, and config.rs, registry.rs, and the daemon's state.rs each open-code their own. Function-scoped rather than whole-file so the rest of the module stays scanned, including the three-way read classification and the age arithmetic the surfaces render, and so any newly added filesystem primitive here fails the guard until it is justified.

Durable bookkeeping marker published beside the last-admission marker, not an answer authority.
